prompt: Match each step to the question it answers.

pairs.right: who do you claim to be?

prompt: Typing "ana" in the username box is which step?

choices.text: Accounting of the visit
choices.why: Accounting records what was done afterwards.

choices.text: Authorisation to use the portal
choices.why: Permission comes after proof.

choices.text: Identification: a bare claim
choices.why: Right. A claim anybody can type.

choices.text: Authentication, since the system now knows who it is
choices.why: Nothing has been proved yet.

prompt: Why must authentication come before authorisation?
hint: What does a rule about "your own payslip" need?

choices.text: Because passwords are slower to check than rules
choices.why: Speed has nothing to do with it.

choices.text: The rules need to know who the person is
choices.why: Right. "Yours" means nothing until the system knows who you are.

choices.text: It does not; either order works the same
choices.why: The rule cannot be evaluated without an identity.

choices.text: Because authorisation grants the password
choices.why: Authorisation never grants a password.

prompt: Authentication, authorisation and accounting together are called ___.
Which HTTP status code means "I know who you are, and you may not"?
A request with no password got 401 and a WWW-Authenticate header. What was the portal saying?

choices.text: The payslip does not exist
choices.why: That would be 404.

choices.text: The server is down and cannot answer
choices.why: It answered.

choices.text: You may not read this, whoever you are
choices.why: That would be 403, after knowing who.

choices.text: I don't know who you are yet; here is how to prove it
choices.why: Right. 401 asks for authentication.

prompt: bruno, in hr, read ana's payslip; ana could not read bruno's. Which step made the difference?

choices.text: Accounting, since bruno's requests were logged
choices.why: Both were logged.

choices.text: Authentication, since bruno's password is stronger
choices.why: Both authenticated successfully.

choices.text: Identification, because bruno typed his name first
choices.why: Order of typing is irrelevant.

choices.text: Authorisation
choices.why: Right. The rules treat the hr role differently.

prompt: For carla, who does not exist, ana got 403 and bruno got 404. What would ana learn if the portal checked existence first?

choices.text: bruno's salary
choices.why: The 403 shows no payslip contents.

choices.text: The hr group's password
choices.why: Groups have no password here.

choices.text: Nothing more, since she is refused either way
choices.why: The code would differ by name, and that is information.

choices.text: Which names are on the payroll
choices.why: Right. A refusal must not answer a question she may not ask.

prompt: In the code, what does who() returning nothing lead to?

choices.text: The payslip is served to an anonymous user
choices.why: The function returns before reaching that line.

choices.text: A 403, because the user is not in hr
choices.why: The hr check comes later, after identity is known.

choices.text: A 404, because no payslip is found
choices.why: Existence is checked last.

choices.text: It calls ask_to_sign_in(), which answers 401
choices.why: Right. No identity, no further checks.

prompt: Put the portal's checks in the order the code makes them.
items: may they read this payslip (403 if not)
does the payslip exist (404 if not)
trap: Checking existence before permission would tell a refused user which payslips exist.

prompt: A page hides the link to other people's payslips. Why does the lesson say that is not authorisation?

choices.text: Browsers show hidden links anyway, in the page source
choices.why: They do not; that is not the reason.

choices.text: Hidden links slow the page down
choices.why: Speed is not the issue.

choices.text: The server never checked; anyone types the address
choices.why: Right. Hiding a button is design, not a control.

choices.text: Links are encrypted and cannot be hidden
choices.why: Encryption is unrelated.

prompt: Match each rule to the access control model it belongs to.

pairs.left: bruno shares his folder with ana
members of hr may read any payslip
staff may read the handbook from a managed device in working hours
only people cleared for confidential read confidential files

choices.text: More roles than people
choices.why: Right. The model stops being simple.

choices.text: A role that grants every permission at once
choices.why: That is a badly designed role, not explosion.

choices.text: Roles expiring at the end of the year
choices.why: Roles do not expire by default.

choices.text: An attacker deleting all the roles
choices.why: Not what the term means.

prompt: The portal's rule is: yours, or you are in hr. How does the lesson classify it?

choices.text: RBAC for the hr half, ABAC for the owner half
choices.why: Right. Two models in one line is the normal case.

choices.text: Pure DAC, because each user owns a payslip
choices.why: Owners do not decide who else reads; the portal does.

choices.text: None, since it is just an if statement
choices.why: Every model ends up as code like this.

choices.text: MAC, because the portal enforces it centrally
choices.why: There are no clearance labels.

prompt: Which category did the OWASP Top 10 put first in its 2021 edition?

choices.text: Weak passwords and reused credentials
choices.why: Authentication failures are on the list, not first.

choices.text: Missing backups
choices.why: Not an OWASP web category.

choices.text: Slow pages
choices.why: Not a security category.

choices.text: Broken access control
choices.why: Right. Almost every case confuses the two questions.

prompt: Any signed-in user can change /payslips/ana to /payslips/bruno and read it. What is this flaw called?
hint: The address refers directly to an object.

choices.text: A zero-day in the web server
choices.why: It is a missing check in the application.

choices.text: Privilege creep, from a long-serving user
choices.why: Any user can do it on day one.

choices.text: A weak password policy
choices.why: Every user here has authenticated properly.

choices.text: Insecure direct object reference (IDOR)
choices.why: Right. Nobody asked whether this user may have that object.

prompt: The log shows a sharp rise in 403s for one account. What does the lesson suggest it points to?
hint: The account proved who it was.

choices.text: A wrong role, or somebody exploring
choices.why: Right. Authenticated and asking for what it may not have.

choices.text: The server running out of disk space
choices.why: That is not what 403 signals.

choices.text: Someone guessing that account's password
choices.why: Failed guesses produce 401s.

choices.text: The password database being down
choices.why: Then nobody would authenticate.

prompt: Which of these are authorisation decisions? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: the password matches the stored hash
choices.why: That is authentication.

choices.text: hr may read any payslip
choices.why: A rule about permission.

choices.text: ana may run tail on the portal's log as root
choices.why: lesson 6's sudo rule.

choices.text: the request is written to the log
choices.why: That is accounting.

prompt: A new export page checks that the user is signed in and returns the whole customer list. Which mistake from the lesson is it?

choices.text: Role explosion in the hr group
choices.why: Roles are not involved; the page checks none.

choices.text: A missing check on one path
choices.why: Right. Access control fails at its weakest page.

choices.text: Mandatory access control being too strict
choices.why: The page is far too loose, not strict.

choices.text: A leak through error messages
choices.why: No error message is involved.
